paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples should receive labels. This paper asks how that choice should change with the labeling budget. Its theoretical analysis identifies a transition: representative examples are preferable when labels are scarce, whereas less representative examples become preferable when the budget is large. Combined evidence suggests a similar pattern in common classification models.

The authors turn this finding into TypiClust, a deep active learning strategy designed for small budgets. The central idea is that selecting useful examples depends on how much labeled information the learner already has. A strategy that works well after many labels have been collected may therefore be poorly suited to the beginning of learning.

In supervised experiments across image datasets and architectures, TypiClust outperforms the other strategies tested in the low-budget setting. Its gains are larger when combined with semi-supervised learning. On CIFAR-10, semi-supervised methods using ten TypiClust-selected labels reach 93.2% accuracy. These findings support choosing an acquisition strategy with the available budget explicitly in mind.
icml-2022-active-learning-on-a-budget-op.tldr: TypiClust exploits the finding that representative examples are especially valuable when an active learner has very few labels.

paragraphs: Gaussian process bandits guide sequential searches for good inputs to functions whose evaluations are expensive or noisy. This paper examines what happens when an adversary deliberately interferes with that search. It takes the attacker's perspective, studying how manipulation can steer an optimizer toward a chosen region rather than merely making its observations less reliable.

The attacks primarily target GP-UCB and a related elimination-based algorithm. They perturb the objective so that the resulting function has its optima in the attacker's target region. The authors distinguish attackers who know the original function from those who do not. Their theoretical analysis motivates Subtraction and Clipping attacks for the former setting and an Aggressive subtraction attack for the latter.

Experiments across diverse objective functions show that targeted steering can succeed even with a small attack budget. The contribution is both analytical and practical: it connects different levels of attacker knowledge and strength to concrete attacks. The findings demonstrate possible vulnerabilities under the studied conditions, rather than establishing that every Gaussian process optimizer can always be redirected.
icml-2022-adversarial-attacks-on-gaussia.tldr: Targeted attacks can steer Gaussian process bandit algorithms toward an adversary's chosen region, sometimes with a small attack budget.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning usually assumes that an agent receives an exact description of the state it should reach. This paper addresses situations where that configuration is unavailable before acting. Instead, the intended framework lets an agent receive an example of an analogous task and infer a suitable goal for its own current situation.

The authors introduce goal-conditioned bisimulation, a form of state abstraction that captures functional equivariance. The purpose is to represent relationships that let a skill remain useful when the particular state and goal change. They learn the representation through a metric version of the abstraction, connecting the formal notion of task similarity to a representation that an agent can use.

The learned representation generalizes to new goals in real-world manipulation tasks. The paper also proves a broader sufficiency result: the representation supports goal-conditioned tasks and downstream tasks whose rewards depend only on state. That reward restriction defines the stated scope of the broader result. Together, the findings connect learning by analogy with a formal account of reusable representations.
icml-2022-bisimulation-makes-analogies-i.tldr: Goal-conditioned bisimulation learns representations that support skill reuse and generalization to new goals through task analogies.

paragraphs: This paper changes the mathematical objects used as neural network parameters. It replaces ordinary numerical parameters with values in a C*-algebra, a structure that generalizes complex numbers. One example is a space of continuous functions on a compact space. This makes function-valued parameters part of the framework, rather than treating every parameter as a single number.

The generalization allows multiple models to be combined continuously. It also opens the door to operations associated with functions, including regression and integration. The authors use these capabilities to learn data features efficiently and adapt models continuously across problems. The significance lies in giving model combination and adaptation a shared mathematical setting.

Applications to density estimation and few-shot learning show that the framework can learn features with limited samples. These demonstrations support the usefulness of the proposed parameterization in the studied problems. The broader conclusion remains exploratory: the work points to the potential of C*-algebra theory for general neural network models, rather than establishing that this parameterization improves every architecture or task.
icml-2022-c-algebra-net-a-new-approach-g.tldr: C*-algebra-valued parameters enable continuous model combination and show promise for learning useful features from limited data.

paragraphs: Information-directed sampling chooses actions by balancing their immediate consequences against the information they provide. When a decision also comes with context, the appropriate information objective becomes less obvious. This paper asks whether exploration should be evaluated only for the context currently observed or in relation to the distribution of contexts the agent may encounter.

The authors study contextual bandits with graph feedback and sparse linear contextual bandits. In these settings, they prove an advantage for contextual IDS over conditional IDS. The key distinction is that information gathered now can help with future contexts. A method focused too narrowly on the present context can undervalue actions whose benefits appear in later, different situations.

The paper also develops a computationally efficient contextual IDS implementation based on Actor-Critic and evaluates it on a neural network contextual bandit. This connects the theoretical design principle to a practical algorithm. The central finding is that context distribution belongs in the exploration calculation: an informative action should be assessed partly by how it prepares the learner for contexts it has not yet seen.
icml-2022-contextual-information-directe.tldr: Contextual IDS improves exploration by valuing information that can help with future contexts, beyond the context currently observed.

paragraphs: DNA storage requires grouping retrieved DNA sequences according to their similarity. The paper identifies Levenshtein distance as particularly suitable for comparing these sequences, but costly to compute and awkward to combine with established clustering algorithms. This creates a practical bottleneck between recovering sequences and organizing them into useful groups.

The proposed solution learns a vector representation of each sequence. It combines a Siamese neural network, squared Euclidean embedding, and chi-squared regression so that the squared distance between two vectors approximates the sequences' Levenshtein distance. Sequence comparison can then use vector arithmetic, while clustering can operate in a representation better matched to familiar algorithms.

The approach matters because it seeks to retain the useful similarity information of the original distance while changing how that information is computed and consumed. The authors analyze the embedding theoretically and experimentally, reporting efficiency and robustness. The result is an approximation rather than an exact replacement for Levenshtein distance, with the stated findings supporting its usefulness for the DNA sequence clustering step.
icml-2022-deep-squared-euclidean-approxi.tldr: A learned DNA sequence embedding approximates Levenshtein distance with fast squared Euclidean comparisons suited to clustering.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, different labels can depend on different aspects of the same example. Existing label-specific feature methods typically identify the features most useful for each label and train a classifier using those features. This paper develops another way to express the same need for label-dependent discrimination.

Its approach identifies features that are uninformative for a particular label and makes that label's prediction insensitive to changes in them. The proposed method, DELA, uses perturbations to encourage this stability while also identifying the non-informative features. Training is formulated through a probabilistically relaxed expected-risk objective, linking feature identification and classifier behavior within one optimization problem.

This perspective matters because relevance can be expressed through what a classifier should ignore as well as through what it should use. The invariance is label-specific: the method does not require every label to disregard the same features. Experiments on ten benchmark datasets show better performance than the state-of-the-art comparison methods. Those results support learning label-specific resistance to irrelevant variation as an effective strategy for multi-label prediction.
icml-2022-dual-perspective-of-label-spec.tldr: DELA improves multi-label classification by learning which features each label should ignore and making predictions insensitive to their variation.

paragraphs: Training decision trees to withstand adversarial changes can be computationally expensive, and some existing methods lack provable robustness guarantees. This paper aims to address both issues together. It introduces Fast Provably Robust Decision Tree, or FPRDT, with reported computational complexity of O(n log n).

FPRDT balances global and local optimization of the adversarial 0/1 loss, which evaluates classification mistakes under adversarial conditions. This tradeoff is central to making robust training efficient. The authors then build a boosting method, PRAdaBoost, from these robust trees and analyze convergence of its training adversarial 0/1 loss. The contribution therefore covers both individual trees and their combination into an ensemble.

Experiments support the proposed methods on performance and speed. They outperform the compared methods without provable robustness and achieve better or comparable performance to the compared provably robust methods, with the shortest reported running time. These findings suggest that robustness guarantees and practical training efficiency can coexist in the studied tree-based approaches, rather than requiring the computational costs associated with the comparison methods.
icml-2022-fast-provably-robust-decision-.tldr: FPRDT and PRAdaBoost combine provable adversarial robustness with efficient tree training and strong comparative experimental performance.

paragraphs: Mixup creates training examples by interpolating between existing samples and their labels. Applying that idea directly to graphs is difficult because graphs can have different numbers of nodes, lack a natural alignment, and have different connectivity structures. This paper moves the interpolation to a representation of how graphs are generated.

G-Mixup first estimates a graphon for each class using graphs belonging to that class. A graphon acts as a graph generator. The method interpolates between these class generators in Euclidean space and then samples synthetic graphs from the resulting mixed generator. It therefore constructs new graphs without requiring a direct correspondence between the nodes of two individual input graphs.

The approach matters because it gives graph augmentation a shared space in which mixing is feasible despite differences in graph size and structure. Extensive experiments report substantial improvements in the generalization and robustness of graph neural networks. These results support generator-level interpolation as a useful way to bring mixup's benefits to graph classification, where ordinary sample-level interpolation is difficult to define.
icml-2022-g-mixup-graph-data-augmentatio.tldr: G-Mixup augments graph datasets by mixing class-level graph generators and sampling new graphs from the mixtures.

paragraphs: Books, images, and music can contain very long sequences of elements, making their long-range structure expensive for conventional autoregressive Transformers to model. Perceiver AR addresses this computational problem with an architecture intended to work across modalities. Its aim is to make long-context probability modeling practical while retaining the ordering required for autoregressive generation.

The architecture uses cross-attention to map a long input sequence into a smaller collection of latent representations. It maintains causal masking throughout, so predictions respect which inputs are available at each position. This design allows direct attention to more than one hundred thousand tokens without requiring manually designed sparse attention patterns or separate memory mechanisms.

When trained on images and music, Perceiver AR produces samples with clear long-term structure and coherence. It also achieves state-of-the-art likelihood on the reported long-sequence benchmarks, including 64-by-64 ImageNet images and PG-19 books. These findings support the architectural idea that a compact latent representation can make very long input contexts useful for both probability estimation and structured generation.
icml-2022-general-purpose-long-context-a.tldr: Perceiver AR uses cross-attention and compact latents to model long sequences while preserving causal autoregressive prediction.

paragraphs: Robustness certificates aim to establish that a model's predictions withstand specified changes to its input. Existing randomized smoothing defenses have made progress for attacks bounded by mathematical norms, but semantic transformations present a different challenge. The paper highlights operations such as defocus blur and pixelation, especially transformations without convenient closed-form expressions.

GSmooth generalizes randomized smoothing through a dimension augmentation strategy. Within this theoretical framework, the authors develop a scalable algorithm that approximates complex transformations using an image-to-image surrogate network. The surrogate provides a way to study transformation properties and support robustness certification when the transformation itself is difficult to handle analytically.

Experiments on several datasets demonstrate certification against multiple semantic transformations and corruptions that the alternative baselines cannot certify in the reported evaluation. The contribution expands the kinds of input changes that a certification approach can address. Its significance is the connection between a general theoretical framework and a learned approximation of complex transformations, allowing the study to move beyond the norm-bounded perturbations emphasized by earlier defenses.
icml-2022-gsmooth-certified-robustness-a.tldr: GSmooth extends robustness certification to complex semantic transformations using dimension augmentation and learned transformation surrogates.

paragraphs: This paper studies how deep learning shapes solutions in tensor factorization through implicit regularization. The focus is the preference induced by the learning setup itself, rather than an explicitly added regularization term. In particular, the authors examine how this effect changes as the factorization network becomes deeper.

Prior results for deep matrix factorization and shallow tensor factorization describe a preference for low-rank solutions with growth that is at most quadratic. The paper shows that the corresponding effect in deep tensor factorization grows polynomially with network depth. This identifies depth as an important part of the regularization behavior and distinguishes deep tensor factorization from the related settings discussed in the abstract.

The theoretical description closely matches the experimental behavior observed by the authors. Numerical experiments also demonstrate more accurate estimation and better convergence properties associated with the implicit regularization. The contribution connects a mathematical characterization of depth-dependent behavior to practical outcomes in factorization, providing an explanation for the reported experiments rather than only recording that deeper models behave differently.
icml-2022-implicit-regularization-with-p.tldr: Implicit regularization in deep tensor factorization grows polynomially with depth and helps explain improved estimation and convergence in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Continual learning must preserve older knowledge while adapting to new tasks. It should also reuse earlier learning without introducing excessive training overhead or requiring a continually growing model. NISPA addresses these competing goals through a sparse neural network whose connection density stays fixed as learning progresses.

The architecture forms stable paths that retain knowledge from previous tasks. It also rewires connections to create plastic paths that can learn new tasks while reusing existing knowledge. Stability and adaptability are therefore managed through the network's connectivity. Keeping the density fixed makes changing which connections exist a central mechanism for accommodating new learning.

Evaluations on EMNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 show significant improvements over representative state-of-the-art continual learning baselines. NISPA also uses up to ten times fewer learnable parameters than the baselines. These results support sparse rewiring as a practical approach to retaining and extending knowledge. The authors additionally argue that sparsity is essential for continual learning; this is their broader interpretation of the work, beyond the specific empirical comparisons.
icml-2022-nispa-neuro-inspired-stability.tldr: NISPA preserves old knowledge through stable sparse paths and rewires other connections to learn new tasks with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often assumes that rewards are available immediately after actions, but practical tasks may provide feedback only later. This paper formally defines environments with delayed rewards and examines the resulting non-Markovian structure. The difficulty is that the usual current-state description does not fully capture the dependencies introduced by delayed feedback.

The authors propose a general off-policy framework built around a new Q-function formulation. This reformulation is designed to handle delayed rewards and comes with theoretical convergence guarantees. The contribution changes the value-learning framework itself, giving delayed feedback an explicit place in how future outcomes are represented and learned.

For high-dimensional state spaces, the paper introduces an HC-decomposition rule for the Q-function. This leads to a practical approximation scheme intended to improve training efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments report better performance than existing work and the tested variants. The paper thus connects a formal treatment of delayed rewards with a computational approach for larger problems, addressing both the validity of learning updates and their practical behavior during training.
icml-2022-off-policy-reinforcement-learn.tldr: A new off-policy Q-function framework handles delayed rewards, with convergence guarantees and a decomposition for efficient high-dimensional learning.

paragraphs: Bug detectors trained on artificially corrupted programs can perform well on synthetic tests yet produce mostly false alarms in real repositories. The paper cites synthetic test accuracy above 90% alongside real-world precision below 10%. These are different evaluation measures, but the contrast motivates investigating whether the training examples represent real bugs.

The authors attribute the deployment problem to a mismatch between synthetic and real bug distributions. Their solution trains a detector in two phases: synthetic bugs first introduce the detection task, and real bugs then move the model toward the distribution it will encounter in practice. A multi-task hierarchy, focal loss, and contrastive learning further support training.

The evaluation covers three widely studied bug types and introduces datasets designed to reflect real bug distributions. The resulting detectors perform well on both these test sets and the open-source repository versions evaluated. The findings support matching training and evaluation data to deployment conditions, while showing how synthetic examples can remain useful as an initial stage of a more realistic training process.
icml-2022-on-distribution-shift-in-learn.tldr: Training first on synthetic bugs and then on real bugs helps bridge the distribution shift that undermines practical bug detection.

paragraphs: Online continual learning updates a model as new data arrives while trying to preserve what it has already learned. This paper identifies feature bias as one contributor to catastrophic forgetting. Cross-entropy training emphasizes features that distinguish the current task's classes, but those features may be less useful for another task, prompting parameter changes that disrupt earlier knowledge.

The proposed method, OCM, uses mutual information maximization to address two objectives. It encourages each task to draw on a fuller range of features in its training data, reducing reliance on a narrow discriminative subset. It also encourages preservation of previously learned knowledge when the model trains on each new batch of arriving data.

Empirical comparisons show substantial improvements over the evaluated online continual learning baselines. On CIFAR10, OCM raises accuracy from the best baseline's 64.1% to 77.2%, a gain of 13.1 percentage points. The result supports jointly addressing the breadth of learned features and the retention of previous knowledge, rather than treating forgetting solely as a problem arising after a new task arrives.
icml-2022-online-continual-learning-thro.tldr: OCM uses mutual information maximization to learn broader features and preserve prior knowledge as new data arrives.

paragraphs: This paper studies differentially private stochastic convex optimization when observations arrive sequentially and updated parameters are released after each observation. Repeated release makes privacy part of the ongoing learning process. The authors address different norm geometries, where the geometry affects the achievable excess risk, or gap from the best objective value.

Their algorithm is a private Frank-Wolfe variant using recursive gradient estimates to reduce variance. Combined with adaptive privacy analysis, it achieves optimal excess risk in linear time for 1 < p ≤ 2. For 2 < p ≤ infinity, it obtains state-of-the-art excess risk matching non-private lower bounds. An extension to p = 1 achieves nearly dimension-independent excess risk.

The paper also establishes a recursive-gradient variance-reduction guarantee in a non-stationary setting, extending beyond the independent, identically distributed setting covered by previous guarantees. As an application, it develops a differentially private algorithm for high-dimensional generalized linear bandits with logarithmic regret. Together, these results connect private continual parameter release with efficient optimization and sequential decision-making.
icml-2022-private-streaming-sco-in-ell-p.tldr: A private streaming Frank-Wolfe method provides strong excess-risk guarantees under continual release and supports bandit learning with logarithmic regret.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can benefit from efficient feature representations that approximate their kernel functions. This paper introduces such random features for a broad family called Generalized Zonal Kernels. The family extends dot-product kernels on the unit sphere by adding radial factors to their Gegenbauer series expansions, allowing the representation to account for more than direction alone.

The resulting family includes all dot-product kernels, Gaussian kernels, and Neural Tangent kernels. The authors construct random features using randomly oriented Gegenbauer harmonics and their reproducing property. A single mathematical construction therefore covers several widely used kinds of kernels, making the proposed approximation framework broadly applicable within this family.

The paper proves subspace embedding guarantees for the features. These guarantees justify using the approximation to solve learning problems such as kernel k-means and kernel ridge regression approximately. Empirical results also show improvements over recent kernel approximation methods. The contribution combines breadth of kernel coverage with theoretical support for downstream learning, rather than evaluating approximation quality only as an isolated numerical objective.
icml-2022-random-gegenbauer-features-for.tldr: Random Gegenbauer features efficiently approximate a broad kernel family with guarantees supporting approximate clustering and regression.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes assign probabilities to subsets of a collection. Allowing their kernel matrices to be nonsymmetric increases modeling power, but sampling can become expensive. For subsets of a fixed size k, a previous approximate Markov chain Monte Carlo approach takes time quadratic in the number of available items, limiting large-scale use.

The authors develop a scalable sampler for fixed-size nonsymmetric DPPs with low-rank kernels. It builds on rejection sampling and introduces an efficient way to construct the proposal distribution. Under this low-rank setting, runtime becomes sublinear in the number of items. The kernel assumption is therefore central to the stated improvement in scalability.

They also extend the algorithm to subsets without a fixed size. The resulting method has polynomial dependence on kernel rank, replacing the exponential rank dependence of the existing approach. Theoretical analysis and real-world dataset experiments support the methods, with reported speedups of orders of magnitude. These are approximate sampling algorithms, providing a more scalable route to using the richer nonsymmetric models.
icml-2022-scalable-mcmc-sampling-for-non.tldr: Low-rank structure and efficient proposal construction make approximate sampling from nonsymmetric DPPs substantially more scalable.

paragraphs: Importance sampling changes how component functions are sampled during stochastic optimization. It can improve the problem's conditioning or reduce noise in the estimated gradient. This paper focuses on the second benefit, asking how sampling alone can yield a practical method with a provable improvement in the long-run error of stochastic gradient descent.

The proposed stochastic reweighted gradient descent method, SRG, uses importance sampling to reduce gradient-estimation variance. For strongly convex, smooth problems, it can improve asymptotic error relative to SGD. Those mathematical assumptions define the setting of the stated guarantee. The authors also extend SRG to combine variance reduction with importance-sampling-based preconditioning.

The combined algorithm can reduce both the condition number and the asymptotic error, each by up to the number of component functions. This is an upper extent of possible improvement, rather than a uniform gain for every problem. Experiments on regularized logistic regression demonstrate improved convergence in practice, supporting the idea that carefully chosen sampling can address both optimization geometry and gradient noise.
icml-2022-stochastic-reweighted-gradient.tldr: SRG uses importance sampling to reduce gradient variance and can improve both conditioning and asymptotic error in strongly convex, smooth optimization.

paragraphs: People may change their observable attributes when a machine learning model influences consequential decisions about them. Such strategic responses shift the data distribution after deployment. This paper identifies a potential benefit of that shift: the responses can help recover causal relationships between observed features and outcomes, even when unobserved confounders are present.

The authors connect this setting to instrumental variable regression. A sequence of deployed models serves as an instrument because it changes people's observable features without directly changing their outcomes. This separation is central to the proposed causal recovery mechanism. The variation induced by different assessment rules can therefore provide information beyond the correlations in a fixed training dataset.

The paper shows how recovered causal relationships can improve individual fairness, agent outcomes, and predictive risk. Its fairness result is conditional: when people differ in their ability to change non-causal attributes, a decision rule departing from causal coefficients can produce potentially unbounded individual unfairness. The work thus links strategic behavior, causal estimation, and decision quality through one analytical framework.
icml-2022-strategic-instrumental-variabl.tldr: Strategic responses to deployed models can act as instrumental-variable evidence for recovering causal relationships and improving decisions.

paragraphs: Model predictive control can use a learned environment model to plan actions, offering potential advantages in sample efficiency and benefits from additional planning computation. However, long planning horizons are costly, and accurate environment models are difficult to learn. TD-MPC combines short-horizon model-based planning with a learned estimate of longer-term value.

The method learns a task-oriented dynamics model in a latent representation and uses it for local trajectory optimization over a short horizon. At the end of that horizon, a terminal value function estimates the return that remains. Temporal difference learning trains the dynamics model and value function jointly, connecting the model used for near-term planning with the value estimate used beyond it.

Experiments on continuous-control tasks from DMControl and Meta-World cover both state-based and image-based observations. TD-MPC achieves better sample efficiency and asymptotic performance than the compared prior work. These findings support dividing the planning problem between explicit short-term trajectory optimization and learned long-term evaluation, reducing reliance on costly long-horizon planning while retaining a model-based component.
icml-2022-temporal-difference-learning-f.tldr: TD-MPC jointly learns a latent dynamics model and terminal value function to combine short-horizon planning with long-term return estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimating a distribution from samples using piecewise polynomials. The benchmark is the best approximation with a chosen number of pieces and polynomial degree, measured by l1 distance. The objective is to produce an estimate whose error is essentially within a small constant factor of that benchmark.

Except for the single-piece, degree-zero case, the smallest possible factor is at least two. Existing efficient methods had larger guarantees, especially at higher degrees. TURF supplies a near-linear-time estimator that is essentially sample-optimal and establishes the factor of two across all the remaining piece-count and degree combinations. It therefore closes the stated gap between achievable efficient guarantees and the lower bound.

The paper also addresses choosing the number of polynomial pieces, since suitable choices can differ greatly between practical distributions. Its selection method estimates that number near-optimally, helping the estimator approach the best available approximation. Experiments combining estimation and piece-count selection improve on existing methodologies. The contribution joins an optimal approximation factor with computational efficiency and adaptation of model complexity.
icml-2022-turf-two-factor-universal-robu.tldr: TURF achieves the optimal factor-two piecewise-polynomial distribution approximation guarantee with near-linear runtime and near-optimal piece-count selection.

paragraphs: Entity alignment seeks corresponding entities across knowledge graphs. Many embedding-based methods assume that a small set of known matches can anchor the two graphs' representation spaces. This paper examines that assumption by extracting a common paradigm from existing methods and analyzing what their scoring functions actually constrain.

The analysis shows that a predefined scoring margin implicitly bounds the embedding discrepancy between potentially matching entities. However, this bound is not guaranteed to be tight enough for alignment learning. This identifies a gap between imposing a mathematical constraint on the representations and ensuring that the constraint is sufficiently informative for finding matches.

The proposed NeoEA method explicitly learns embeddings intended to be invariant across knowledge graphs. Alongside bringing aligned entities geometrically closer, it aligns embedding distributions and underlying ontology knowledge, described as aligning the graphs' neural ontologies. Experiments show consistent, significant improvements over the best-performing comparison methods. The work combines a diagnosis of an existing assumption with a method that addresses alignment at the distribution and ontology levels as well as through entity distances.
icml-2022-understanding-and-improving-kn.tldr: NeoEA improves entity alignment by addressing weaknesses in anchor-based embedding constraints and aligning distributions and ontology knowledge.

paragraphs: You Only Cut Once, or YOCO, changes how an image augmentation is applied. It splits an image into two pieces and augments each piece individually. This gives each training sample more varied transformations and encourages a network to recognize objects when only part of their visual information is available.

The method is parameter-free and designed to work easily with existing augmentations. Its main contribution is a simple change in the level at which those operations act: separate image regions can receive their own augmentation. The authors evaluate this idea across different augmentation methods and neural network architectures, reporting classification improvements on CIFAR and ImageNet, sometimes by large margins.

YOCO also benefits contrastive pre-training, producing representations that transfer more effectively to multiple downstream tasks in the experiments. The paper studies several variants and analyzes their performance under different settings. Together, these findings show that the way an augmentation is distributed within an image can matter, and that a single cut can improve both direct classification training and representation learning.
icml-2022-you-only-cut-once-boosting-dat.tldr: YOCO improves image augmentation by cutting each image in two and independently augmenting its pieces.
